newsitem.title: USA: Wells Fargo president to retire.
newsitem.headline: Wells Fargo president to retire.

text.p: William Zuendt, one of the architects of Wells Fargo & Co.'s $11 billion acquisition of First Interstate Bancorp, said Wednesday he plans to retire later this year.
Zuendt's departure comes at difficult time for Wells Fargo as it faces continued troubles in integrating First Interstate Bancorp, which it acquired in 1996.

"I'm disappointed that we have had more customer impact than we expected. I think the company is still figuring out how to run itself now that it's twice as big and has two cultures," Zuendt, 50, said.

Zuendt, who is president and chief operating officer of the San Francisco-based banking giant, planned to retire earlier, but kept postponing his decision due to challenges that developed throughout the 1990s, including the merger with First Interstate.
"Now that we've acquired First Interstate and merged the two organisations, the timing seems right," he said.
Zuendt recalled some difficult times, including disruptions to the company's automated telephone banking system in September, which caused many customer complaints.

While integration of the two banks' systems is now virtually complete, he said some challenges remain in converting First Interstate's 13-state franchise into one national bank and stemming the departure of customers.
"Doing a merger is distracting and takes your eye off the customer," he said.

Wells Fargo stock fell $7.625 to $258 a share on the New York Stock Exchange. Other banks also slipped on profit-taking after posting gains Tuesday on the Federal Reserve Board's decision to leave interest rates alone.
In Zuendt's place, effective immediately, four vice chairmen will form a team with Chairman Paul Hazen as part of a newly created Office of the Chairman, with three customer segments.
Zuendt, who will resign from the board in July, said he will travel extensively after he retires and does not plan to return to banking.
"Technology has always been one of my real interests," said the executive, who earned $600,000 in 1996 plus a bonus of $1.2 million and other compensation.
He joined Wells Fargo in 1973 with responsibility for its computer systems and operations.

In 1980, he was elected an executive vice president and moved to the retail banking division, where he directed the bank's strategy throughout the decade. He became vice chairman in 1986, and president in January 1995.
Zuendt replaced Hazen as president in 1995 when Hazen took the helm as chairman and chief executive officer, succeeding Carl Reichardt.
While Zuendt's retirement was anticipated, analysts said the executive would be missed during this critical juncture for the bank.
"There was a high comfort level with Zuendt (on Wall Street). He will be missed," said Brown Brothers Harriman analyst Raphael Soifer.
The banking giant is about halfway through a massive cost-cutting programme, but is losing many customers due to the integration, which is hurting its earnings and revenues prospects.

The announcement of Zuendt's retirement came on the heels of news earlier this week that Berkshire Hathaway Inc., headed by billionaire Warren Buffett, cut its stake in Wells Fargo to about 7 million shares or about 7.6 percent from 8 percent previously held.
Comprising the new Office of the Chairman, will be Vice Chairman Terri Dial, 47; Vice Chairman Clyde Ostler, 50; Charlie Johnson, 55, and Vice Chairman and Chief Financial Officer Rod Jacobs, 56.
